title: Who insures a ship
description: Marine insurance is a stack of separate covers written by separate parties, and a loss is denied at the seams between them far more often than it is denied outright. This dataset names the institutions, attributes cover to individual attacked hulls where the market let it become public, and records who was refused. It is deliberately as much a map of what is not disclosed as of what is: five of the vessels here have no identifiable insurer at all, and that is the finding, not a failure to find one.

layers.covers: Physical loss or damage to the ship itself, from ordinary marine perils — grounding, collision, fire, heavy weather.
layers.excludes: War, strikes, terrorism and malicious acts are struck out by the standard war exclusion and bought back separately.
layers.who_writes_it: Commercial insurers and Lloyd's syndicates, on a slip with a lead and following lines.
layers.note: This is the layer most people mean by 'the ship's insurance', and it is the one that does not answer a missile.

layers.covers: The bought-back perils — war, civil war, revolution, capture, seizure, mines, terrorism and malicious acts. Priced as a percentage of hull value for a period, typically seven days, not per voyage or per year.
layers.excludes: Detainment by reason of customs or trading infringements, and — the live question — losses the insurer can characterise as falling under a different exclusion.
layers.who_writes_it: Lloyd's syndicates, specialist MGAs such as Vessel Protect and Navium Marine, war risk mutuals such as DNK, and several P&I clubs writing primary hull war in their own right.
layers.who_pays: Under most time and voyage charters the charterer bears the additional premium, which is why the charterer is often the party with the budget.
layers.note: A vessel entering a Joint War Committee listed area must notify its insurers, who may charge an additional premium or decline. Eternity C is what happens when they decline.

layers.covers: Third-party liabilities — crew injury and death, pollution, wreck removal, cargo claims, collision liability. Mutual, not commercial: the members are the insurers.
layers.excludes: War risks, which fall to a separate excess war P&I cover.
layers.who_writes_it: The twelve clubs of the International Group, covering about 87% of the world's ocean-going tonnage, plus fixed-premium providers outside it.
layers.who_pays: The shipowner, through calls rather than premiums.
layers.note: Sounion is the clean illustration: the vessel was entered with Gard, and Gard carried no exposure, because the loss was a war risk.

layers.covers: Third-party war liabilities above the primary layer. $500m each event for owners in 2026/27, inclusive of interest and costs.
layers.excludes: Automatic cessation on outbreak of war between any of the UK, USA, France, Russia and China — the five-powers clause.
layers.who_writes_it: The International Group clubs, reinsured through the group programme.
layers.who_pays: Included in the mutual entry, free and unlimited.
layers.note: The minimum excess is the ship's proper value or $500m, whichever is the lesser — so the owner must buy primary war cover to that level and is deemed to have it. This is the layer that survived the 2026 cancellations untouched, and the reason 'P&I clubs cancelled war cover' was wrong.

layers.covers: Lost earnings while the ship is out of service.
layers.excludes: Depends entirely on the wording. On the Nordic Plan it requires a 'state power', which is the ground on which Codan is reported to have refused the Galaxy Leader claim.
layers.note: The layer where the Houthis' legal status — state power, terrorist, or neither — turns into money.

layers.covers: The goods, not the ship. Separate policy, separate insurer, often a separate broker.
layers.excludes: War cover bought back separately, as for hull.
layers.who_writes_it: Cargo underwriters — the largest line in the global marine market at 56.7% of premium.
layers.who_pays: Whoever bears risk in the cargo under the sale contract.
layers.note: Cargo war cover is where affiliation exclusions bit hardest in 2026: Ascot and Navium restricted war cargo cover for Saudi-linked ships in July.

layers.covers: Ransom payment, negotiator fees and crew repatriation.
layers.excludes: Varies; heavily bespoke and rarely discussed publicly.
layers.who_writes_it: Predominantly Lloyd's, plus MGAs bundling it with war risk.
layers.note: The most secretive layer in the stack. The Abdullah's $5m ransom was arranged by a UK P&I club that no source has ever named.

layers.covers: The financing bank, where the owner's own policy fails to respond.
layers.excludes: Depends on why the owner's cover failed.
layers.who_writes_it: Commercial insurers, placed by specialist brokers.
layers.note: Usually invisible. It surfaced in the Vyssos judgment, which is the only complete insurance chain in this dataset available from a primary court document.

vessel_cover.note: LPG tanker, Gulf of Aden. Cameroon-flagged, Indian-owned, 31 years old, detained in Istanbul in January 2025 with 13 deficiencies. The shadow-fleet profile in one hull.

underwriters.name: The American Club
underwriters.note: AM Best B+ stable. Managers Shipowners Claims Bureau Inc, CEO Dorothea Ioannou. Free reserves $48.3m GAAP / $65m statutory at 31 Dec 2025. Cancelled non-mutual Gulf war cover on 1 March 2026 and reinstated on a buy-back basis on 10 March.

underwriters.name: Britannia
underwriters.note: The oldest club in the group. Managed externally by Tindall Riley. 250 members. Free reserves $572.2m. S&P A, outlook cut to negative. Paid the Maryland settlement for the DALI / Baltimore bridge allision.

underwriters.name: Gard
underwriters.note: The largest club, and the first past 300m GT. In-house managed, HQ Arendal. Equity $1,745m. Its CEO Rolf Thore Roppestad chairs the International Group and signed the March 2026 war-risk cancellation circular.

underwriters.name: Japan P&I Club
underwriters.note: Free reserves about $304m. Combined ratio 82.1%, the best in the group. S&P BBB+, outlook raised to positive July 2026.

underwriters.name: London P&I Club
underwriters.note: Writes primary hull war in its own right, with separate limits unrestricted by the ship's insured hull value and war P&I to $500m. Free reserves $192.4m. Withdrew southern Red Sea war components in August 2026.

underwriters.name: NorthStandard
underwriters.note: Formed by the 2023 merger of North and the Standard Club — the reason the group has twelve members and not thirteen. Free reserves $923m.

underwriters.name: The Shipowners' Club
underwriters.note: By far the most vessels of any club — 35,378 across 8,296 members — because it specialises in smaller tonnage. Best combined ratio in the group at 99.6%.

underwriters.name: Skuld
underwriters.note: Took a 12.5% line on the Galaxy Leader hull war slip — a P&I club acting as a hull war underwriter. Contingency reserves $659m, combined ratio 96% net.

underwriters.name: Steamship Mutual
underwriters.note: Record free reserves of $578m. Customarily the first club to announce its general increase, and announced the highest for 2026 at 8%.

underwriters.name: The Swedish Club
underwriters.note: Free reserves $270m. Its 2026 war terms extend standard cover to cyber-related war risks on a portfolio aggregate basis — the only club found to have done so.

underwriters.name: UK P&I Club
underwriters.note: Managed externally by Thomas Miller. Record free reserves $586m. Principal-entity domicile is genuinely unresolved between the UK and Bermuda in public sources.

underwriters.name: West of England
underwriters.note: Writes 'West War', a comprehensive primary war risks product, and will lead or follow on brokers' slips. Record free reserves $376.8m, up 23%. Combined ratio 98%. Tonnage not published.

underwriters.name: DNK — Den Norske Krigsforsikring for Skib
underwriters.note: 457 members, 3,244 vessels and mobile units, total value insured $271bn at 31 December 2025. Writes on the Nordic Marine Insurance Plan and uniquely retains Major Powers War cover, which continues when all conventional insurance automatically terminates.

underwriters.name: Hellenic War Risks
underwriters.note: Managed by Thomas Miller. Claims to cover about 80% of all Greek-owned ships and over 3,100 vessels, but the figures on its site carry no as-at date.

underwriters.name: UK War Risks
underwriters.note: PRA-authorised, managed by Thomas Miller. 878 international vessels, undated.

underwriters.name: Norwegian Hull Club
underwriters.note: Represented on the Joint War Committee through Andrew Hannay. Returned 12% of premium, $19.1m, for a sixth consecutive year. S&P A.

underwriters.name: Ingosstrakh
underwriters.note: Was Russia's largest marine-risk provider. Designated by the UK on 13 June 2024 and by OFAC on 10 January 2025 for insuring tankers carrying Russian petroleum. Discloses none of its insured vessels. Remains on some flag states' approved-insurer lists despite sanctions.

underwriters.name: Maritime Mutual Insurance Association
underwriters.note: Not an International Group club. Insured almost one in six of all Western-sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers; 231 covered since 2018. Revenue grew from $14.2m in 2018 to $108.5m in 2024. Reinsured through Lloyd's — Munich Re, Hannover Re, MS Amlin and Atrium named. Offices searched by New Zealand police in October 2025.

underwriters.name: Romarine AS
underwriters.note: Never registered as an insurer. Ordered to halt operations by Norway's Finanstilsynet in March 2025 after issuing certificates for more than 30 sanctioned tankers, one forged on the regulator's own letterhead.

underwriters.name: Seaguard P&I
underwriters.note: Does not exist as a commercial entity. Its listed address in Pinneberg is a residential apartment block. Issued certificates for at least five tankers.

underwriters.name: Ascot
underwriters.note: Took the largest line, 25%, on the Galaxy Leader hull war slip. Its Andrew Moulton chairs the Joint War Committee. In July 2026 told brokers it would not write war cargo cover for Saudi-linked ships.

underwriters.name: Markel
underwriters.note: 20% of the Galaxy Leader slip. The Insurer calls it the lead; Lloyd's List gives Ascot the larger line. Represented on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: Swiss Re
underwriters.note: 15% of the Galaxy Leader slip.

underwriters.name: Arch
underwriters.note: 12.5% of the Galaxy Leader slip.

underwriters.name: Tokio Marine HCC
underwriters.note: 12.5% of the Galaxy Leader slip.

underwriters.name: Ark
underwriters.note: 2.5% of the Galaxy Leader slip.

underwriters.name: Codan
underwriters.note: Loss-of-hire insurer on the Galaxy Leader. Reported to have refused the claim on the ground that the Houthis are not a 'state power' as the Nordic Plan requires.

underwriters.name: Travelers
underwriters.note: The most consequential insurer in this dataset. Led the Tutor war slip and was reported not to have posted salvage security; was Eternity C's annual war-risk insurer and declined to cover its final voyage; and is one of the seven US carriers in the DFC facility.

underwriters.name: Brit — Keel Consortium
underwriters.note: Held 100% of the Sounion war risk and both arranged and funded the salvage. Keel capacity is stated at $120m to $152.5m per risk. Represented on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: Navium Marine
underwriters.note: An MGA led by Clive Washbourn, writing outside the Lloyd's syndicate structure. Held 100% of the True Confidence war risk, reportedly protected by a sidecar with reinsurer Fidelis. In July 2026 restricted cover for Saudi-linked ships.

underwriters.name: Vessel Protect
underwriters.note: Founded 2020, owned by Gallagher, backed 100% by Lloyd's syndicates. Automatic capacity $250m. Held 100% of the Magic Seas war risk and wrote the Vyssos policy on behalf of Lloyd's underwriters. At peak insured almost a third of Ukrainian grain ships.

underwriters.name: AXA XL
underwriters.note: Reported by Lloyd's List and Insurance Day as lead on the Minervagracht war slip. Also leads the International Group's group excess-of-loss reinsurance programme, and is the largest Lloyd's syndicate in marine kidnap and ransom.

underwriters.name: Convex
underwriters.note: Reported by The Insurer as lead on the Minervagracht hull war cover, against Lloyd's List's reading that it holds a follow line behind AXA XL. Represented on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: Beazley
underwriters.note: Syndicates 2623 and 623 reinsured the Vyssos policy. In April 2026 launched a $1bn marine war consortium — $500m hull war and $500m cargo war. Represented on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: Lloyd's Insurance Company SA
underwriters.note: The named insurer in the Vyssos judgment, the only complete insurance chain in this dataset from a primary court document.

underwriters.name: Thomas Miller Specialty
underwriters.note: Fixed-premium P&I on the Rubymar. Told assureds on 13 February 2024 that reinsurers could no longer support war risks in the Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and southern Red Sea from 20 February — two days after Rubymar was hit.

underwriters.name: Chubb
underwriters.note: Lead underwriter of the US DFC maritime facility — it manages the facility, sets pricing and terms, assumes risk, issues policies and handles claims. Also leads a Lloyd's Hormuz consortium of $200m each of hull, P&I and cargo.

underwriters.name: Atrium
underwriters.note: Confirmed it still reinsures Maritime Mutual, after MS Amlin ended its own relationship. Represented on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: MS Amlin
underwriters.note: Confirmed it reinsured Maritime Mutual and has since ended the relationship. Not on the Joint War Committee.

underwriters.name: Tsavliris Salvage Group
underwriters.note: Salvor on the Tutor, engaged on Lloyd's Open Form with SCOPIC declared. The vessel sank before the tugs arrived.

underwriters.name: Ambrey
underwriters.note: Executed the Sounion salvage with more than 200 personnel, seven salvage vessels and three European naval assets over 135 days.

underwriters.name: Joint War Committee
underwriters.note: Underwriting representatives of the Lloyd's and IUA company markets. Chaired by Andrew Moulton of Ascot; secretary Neil Roberts of the LMA. It publishes the Listed Areas circular that turns a geography into a premium — but sets no rates itself: 'rating is a matter for individual negotiation between underwriters and brokers and the JWC plays no role in that.'

underwriters.name: International Group of P&I Clubs
underwriters.note: Twelve clubs covering about 87% of the world's ocean-going tonnage — 1.7bn GT, up from 2.5m GT in 1953. The first Pooling Agreement was signed in 1899. Free reserves reached a record $6.79bn in 2025/26. Chair Rolf Thore Roppestad of Gard; secretariat CEO Nick Shaw.

underwriters.name: International Union of Marine Insurance
underwriters.note: Publishes the global marine premium statistics. Secretary General Lars Lange. Its reading of the March 2026 cancellations is the one to hold: 'a controlled adaptation of risk rather than a withdrawal of capacity.'

underwriters.name: Lloyd's of London
underwriters.note: Calls itself 'a recognised global leader' in war risk and publishes no number for it — no capacity figure, no syndicate count. It does not break out marine at all, reporting Marine, Aviation and Energy as one segment, which ran a 103.5% combined ratio in 2025 on aviation losses. Any quantified Lloyd's Hormuz loss figure did not come from Lloyd's.

underwriters.name: US DFC maritime reinsurance facility
underwriters.note: The US backstop of 2026, and it never insured a single voyage. Announced 6 March 2026 at $20bn and expanded to $40bn on 3 April, using BUILD Act political risk authority rather than MARAD's. Chubb led; Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, Starr and CNA participated. The Congressional Research Service reported on 7 August 2026 that DFC had provided no coverage under the facility; Chubb had said in April that the naval escorts expected to complement it never materialised, making activation infeasible. It was built to solve unavailability of cover. The actual problems were price and crew safety, so it sat idle.

underwriters.name: MARAD war risk insurance, Title XII
underwriters.note: The dormant statutory last resort, and confirmed dormant throughout 2026. Its expiry date was repealed in 2018, so the authority is permanent — there is no sunset to track. It activates only on a finding, with the President's approval, that adequate cover cannot be obtained on reasonable terms from US-authorised companies; the market repriced rather than withdrew, so that gate was never met. It is a live standby facility rather than a dead statute — existing interim binders stay in force without re-application, P&I is capped at $750 per gross ton, and premium rates are fixed only once the event triggers them. It was also built for the wrong war: cover is limited to vessels with a US nexus and is unavailable for the foreign-to-foreign trade that actually needed restarting.

denials.who: Vessels with US, UK or Israeli ownership or 'interest'
denials.what_happened: Warranty clauses requiring 'no US, UK or Israeli involvement' were attached to Red Sea cover across the market. Marcus Baker of Marsh: it is 'just about everybody', and 'it essentially means they won't provide insurance'.
denials.grounds: Affiliation warranty rather than an outright refusal — the commercial effect is the same.
denials.note: Underwriters rarely issue a formal refusal. They attach a warranty, decline the additional premium for a listed area, or cancel on notice. This is the first rung.

denials.who: All vessels, any flag
denials.what_happened: Excluded the Red Sea route entirely from standard marine insurance, regardless of a vessel's provenance.
denials.note: The only named insurer found to have excluded the route outright. It is an Indian insurer — no named London or Lloyd's underwriter has done so publicly on the record.

denials.who: Vessels with US, Israeli or UK links
denials.what_happened: Many underwriters would not offer Middle East cover to US, Israel or UK-linked vessels at any price. One London underwriter said it had no appetite to insure vessels 'even remotely linked' to those three states for a Red Sea passage.
denials.note: High confidence the practice exists — multiple independent reports. Low confidence on attribution: no underwriter is named.

denials.who: Eternity C — Cosmoship Management / Guildford Navigation
denials.what_happened: Declined to extend war-risk cover for the Red Sea passage. The vessel held a baseline annual war-risk policy with Travelers but sailed without the additional cover a Joint War Committee listed area requires. It was sunk by the Houthis the next day; four dead, five missing.
denials.grounds: Heightened risk. Vessels entering a JWC listed area must notify insurers, who may charge an additional premium or decline.
denials.resolved: No litigation by Cosmoship against Travelers found as of September 2026. The loss falls on the owner.
denials.note: The only case found where a named insurer declined cover for a specific vessel that was then destroyed. Lloyd's List headlined it 'Decision swerved big payout'. Eternity C had no direct Israeli link — the operator's other vessels had merely called at Israeli ports. Affiliation-based denial reaching two degrees out. Hull put at $15-20m by the market.

denials.who: Vessels with indirect Israeli ties
denials.what_happened: Israel approached marine insurers about the war-risk status of vessels with indirect Israeli ties, fearing traffic would collapse at Haifa. A maritime security official: vessels will start avoiding Israeli ports not from fear of being hit, but from fear of not being insured.
denials.note: The second-order effect of affiliation warranties: the denial does not have to happen for the deterrent to work.

denials.who: Vessels with any 'Saudi touchpoints', including other flags with past Saudi port calls
denials.by: Ascot and Navium Marine, plus several leading marine war insurers at Lloyd's
denials.what_happened: Told brokers they would not sell war cargo insurance to Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea, and were preparing to cancel existing policies.
denials.grounds: Houthi declaration of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, 20 July 2026, and strikes on the Saudi-flagged tankers Encelia and Layla on 22 July.
denials.note: The first time named Lloyd's syndicates have been publicly identified as restricting by affiliation. Marsh's Marcus Baker said Saudi Arabia may be moving into the same bracket as Israel, the US and the UK. Navium declined to comment; Ascot did not respond.

denials.who: US, UK and Israeli ships
denials.what_happened: Charged three times more than others for Middle East war cover.

denials.who: Ingosstrakh Insurance Company and Alfastrakhovanie Group
denials.what_happened: Designated under Executive Orders 14024 and 13662 on the stated ground that they 'have insured oil tankers transporting Russian petroleum products'. Roughly 180 vessels were listed in the same action.
denials.note: Ingosstrakh was Russia's largest marine-risk provider. The UK had designated it earlier, on 13 June 2024, in its first shadow-fleet package.

denials.who: Ingosstrakh, plus four tankers
denials.what_happened: First UK shadow-fleet designations. Ingosstrakh was at the time Russia's top marine-risk provider.

denials.who: Alfastrakhovanie and VSK, plus 30 ships
denials.what_happened: Two Russian marine insurers designated in what was then the UK's largest dark-fleet action.

denials.who: Persian Gulf Marine Insurance Co and HormuzSafe Marine Services Authority
denials.what_happened: Designated as integral to an Iranian scheme to extract digital assets and other revenue from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz through insurance policies.
denials.note: An insurance product used as an extortion instrument. OFAC has sanctioned more than 100 Iran shadow-fleet vessels since the start of 2026.

denials.who: P&I clubs and their assureds on Russian oil voyages
denials.what_happened: The International Group called the attestation process 'a flawed regime which potentially exposes both the P&I Club and a shipowner, operator, charterer to a breach'. Clubs sit at Tier 3A, without direct access to cargo price information.
denials.grounds: Cover is void for voyages in breach of the cap — set out in the rulebooks of every International Group club.
denials.resolved: Gard, West of England and the American Club each said they would end cover if an attestation proved inaccurate. No documented instance of it actually being pulled.
denials.note: Reuters found five Western insurers — American Club, West of England, Gard, London P&I Club and Maritime Mutual — covering ten Russia-to-Asia voyages in 2024. Neil Roberts of IUMI: 'You're relying on their word.' The cap was lowered from $60 to $47.60 in September 2025.

denials.who: More than 30 sanctioned tankers
denials.by: Norway's Finanstilsynet ordered Romarine AS to halt operations
denials.what_happened: Romarine was never registered as an insurer. It had issued certificates for at least 30 sanctioned tankers, presented to Russian port authorities at Primorsk and De Kastri. A forged document used the financial regulator's own letterhead, cited a non-existent Norwegian law, carried a false stamp and the signature of a person who never worked there.
denials.resolved: Public warning issued 25 March 2025. Oslo police investigated four individuals for forgery and unlicensed insurance mediation.
denials.note: Owned by Andrey Mochalin, a Russian citizen and former employee of Norwegian insurer Hydor AS. Website hosted on a St Petersburg IP. Romarine's explanation for listing sanctioned vessels was 'a technical glitch'.

denials.who: At least five tankers, including the sanctioned Paz and the Deyna
denials.by: Exposed by Ukraine's foreign intelligence service
denials.what_happened: Seaguard P&I of Pinneberg, Germany, does not exist as a commercial entity. Its listed address is a residential apartment block.
denials.note: Bloomberg could not definitively corroborate; Seaguard did not respond. The Deyna was seized by France in March 2026. A reported European Commission investigation rests on a single advocacy-organisation source and is not independently confirmed.

denials.who: Almost one in six of all Western-sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers
denials.by: Maritime Mutual Insurance Association, Auckland — real, and reinsured at Lloyd's
denials.what_happened: Reuters identified 231 tankers covered since 2018. Of those, 97 sanctioned tankers had held cover and 48 were carrying it on the day they were blacklisted. Seven declared Maritime Mutual insurance after being blacklisted. Revenue grew from $14.2m in 2018 to $108.5m in 2024.
denials.resolved: New Zealand police searched its Auckland and Christchurch offices and an Auckland residence on 16 October 2025. No charges filed as of publication. Four days later the board resolved not to cover any vessel identified as shadow fleet by Windward or Lloyd's List, nor any vessel carrying Russian oil or refined products.
denials.note: The largest single enabler found, and not a fake company — reinsured through Lloyd's, with Munich Re, Hannover Re, MS Amlin and Atrium named. MS Amlin confirmed it has ended the relationship; Atrium confirmed it continues. Reuters found no instance of Maritime Mutual ever paying a claim to a sanctioned vessel or owner.

denials.who: All assureds trading Iran and the Persian/Arabian Gulf
denials.by: Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, London P&I Club and the American Club
denials.what_happened: A 72-hour Notice of Cancellation for war risks under clause JL2022-020, effective 00:00 GMT on 5 March 2026. Cover was automatically reinstated at the same instant with a geographic exclusion covering Iranian waters, the Persian/Arabian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and adjacent waters. Roughly 21 non-mutual product lines were affected — charterers' P&I, traders' P&I, fixed-premium and extended crew cover, MOU cover and others.
denials.grounds: Gard's own circular states the cause in its opening sentence: the clubs had themselves received Notice of Cancellation from their reinsurers.
denials.note: Read this precisely. The mutual owned P&I cover and the Excess War P&I reinsurance were untouched — the International Group confirms that cover 'has not been amended' and remains free and unlimited. Lloyd's List published a corrective headlined 'No, P&I clubs have not cancelled war risk cover'. What went was the non-poolable layer, mainly chartered-vessel exposures.

denials.who: All entered tonnage transiting Bab el-Mandeb, the southern Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean
denials.by: London P&I, Skuld, the Swedish Club, NorthStandard, the Shipowners' Club and the UK P&I Club
denials.what_happened: Fixed-premium and non-poolable war-risk components withdrawn, effective around 16 August 2026. The excluded zone was extended north to latitude 25°30'N, capturing most of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coastline — considerably further north than any previous Red Sea restriction. Buy-back was available at renegotiated terms.
denials.grounds: The clubs' commercial reinsurers cancelled the underlying agreements.
denials.note: Triggered by the Tihamah, hit off Al Mokha on 11 August 2026 with several seafarers killed. Lloyd's List reported that syndicates and reinsurance carriers 'pushed home their advantage to secure restrictive warranties'. Saudi-linked ships were then excluded from the buy-back.

denials.who: Saudi-linked tonnage
denials.by: International Group clubs, in the Red Sea buy-back terms
denials.what_happened: Saudi-linked tonnage was explicitly excluded from the Red Sea buy-back cover. Charterers' liability cover remained obtainable, at higher cost.

denials.who: 36.5% of the global tanker fleet — 5,134 vessels
denials.what_happened: The KSE Institute reviewed roughly 14,000 active tankers, 141 flag-state-recognised P&I providers and 42 public databases, and could identify insurance for only 63.5%. Of tankers carrying Russian crude in 2024, just 29.4% had International Group cover, against more than 90% for tankers carrying only non-Russian cargo.
denials.note: Non-IG ships average 18.1 years against 14.4 for IG-insured, and 64.2% sit on grey, black or unranked registries against 25%.

denials.who: Around one third of oil tankers crossing the Baltic
denials.what_happened: In late February 2026, roughly a third of Baltic tanker transits presented insurance certificates from sanctioned Russian or Russian-linked insurers. Separately, more than 90% of shadow-fleet ships produce an insurance certificate when challenged — around 95% of those challenged by Finland and 92% by Estonia.
denials.note: The two figures are not in conflict — they measure paper against substance. Over 90% produce a certificate; 36.5% have no verifiable cover. The gap between a document produced at a Baltic checkpoint and an insurer that would actually pay is the shadow fleet's insurance problem, and Romarine, Seaguard and Maritime Mutual are its three named faces. Sanctioned insurers also remain on some flag states' approved lists.

case_law.issue: Whether aircraft stranded in Russia by Order 311 of 10 March 2022 fell to All Risks or to War Risks insurers, and whether sanctions barred payment.
case_law.held: Order 311 was a 'restraint' or 'detention' within the Government Peril definition, so the claims were excluded from All Risks cover and fell to the War Risks insurers. The loss date was fixed at 10 March 2022. AerCap succeeded under Contingent Cover rather than Possessed Cover because no lessor had taken steps to repossess, and recovered the lower $1.2bn limit of indemnity.
case_law.why_it_matters: Now the leading English authority on war-risk exclusions, after a 50-day trial, and directly analogous to a marine blocking-and-trapping claim. Two points bite on shipping. First, Butcher J indicated obiter that the Wayne Tank principle — where concurrent causes exist and one is excluded, the exclusion prevails — applies to independent concurrent causes as well as interdependent ones, materially widening insurers' ability to defeat a claim on causation. Second, some lessors' war-risk policies contained geographical-limit review provisions under which insurers had terminated Russia cover before the loss. That is precisely the 'we cancelled on notice before the loss' defence now being built into Gulf and Red Sea cover.
case_law.note: On 16 September 2025 Butcher J refused the war-risk insurers permission to appeal on all grounds and ordered payment of interest. AerCap recovers 65% of its costs, roughly £81m.

case_law.case: Oceanus Capital SARL v Lloyd's Insurance Company SA (the Vyssos)
case_law.issue: Whether a mortgagee interest claim for a mine strike in Ukrainian waters failed because of a trading-warranty breach evidenced by forged additional cover.
case_law.held: The proximate cause of the loss was the mine strike, not the forged additional cover. The assured was not privy to the trading-warranty breach because it had relied on fraudulent documentation. Judgment for the claimant.
case_law.why_it_matters: The only complete insurance chain in this dataset that comes from a primary court document rather than trade journalism — insurer, MGA, reinsurers and both brokers are all named in the judgment. It also shows the route by which a forged certificate reaches an English court, which is the shadow-fleet problem arriving in litigation.

case_law.case: Delos Shipholding SA v Allianz Global Corporate & Specialty SE (the Win Win)
case_law.court: English Commercial Court, then Court of Appeal (Males, Asplin and Popplewell LJJ)
case_law.issue: Whether detention by Indonesia for anchoring in Singapore's waters was a fortuity, and whether the owners had made a fair presentation of the risk.
case_law.held: The loss was fortuitous — the anchorage had for many years been used by hundreds if not thousands of vessels without problem. Detention beyond six months made it a constructive total loss. The Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed the insurers' appeal.
case_law.why_it_matters: The most recent appellate confirmation that a war-risks detention claim will be paid where the detention was genuinely unexpected. Written on the American Institute Hull War Risks and Strikes Clauses 1/12/1977, and also the leading recent treatment of the duty of fair presentation in a marine context.

case_law.case: Navigators Insurance v Atlasnavios-Navegação (the B Atlantic)
case_law.issue: Whether cover for 'persons acting maliciously' responded where 132kg of cocaine was strapped to the hull by third parties in Venezuela and the vessel was detained.
case_law.held: The claim failed. Cover for persons acting maliciously was defeated by the exclusion for detainment by reason of infringement of customs regulations. The Court also held that malice requires a mental element of spite or ill-will.
case_law.why_it_matters: The controlling authority on how an exclusion overrides an insured peril in the Institute War and Strikes Clauses. Owners abandoned the vessel after six months' detention and still recovered nothing.

case_law.case: Suez Fortune Investments and Piraeus Bank v Talbot Underwriting (the Brillante Virtuoso)
case_law.issue: Whether a fire in the Gulf of Aden was piracy, or a deliberate scuttling.
case_law.held: The vessel was deliberately scuttled on the instructions of the owners and the beneficial owner in a failed fraud. Piracy was unavailable because the event was not objectively so motivated. War risk insurers denied liability and were vindicated. The innocent co-assured, Piraeus Bank, also lost.
case_law.why_it_matters: The reason underwriters investigate rather than pay a Gulf of Aden total loss on the face of it, and the origin of the 'innocent co-assured's uninsured peril' problem — a financing bank with no involvement in the fraud still recovered nothing.

case_law.case: Gard Marine & Energy v China National Chartering (the Ocean Victory)
case_law.issue: Whether time charterers breached a safe-port warranty when a capesize grounded leaving Kashima and broke in two.
case_law.held: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeal against Gard. It also settled that a charterer cannot limit liability the way an owner can for the loss of a chartered ship.
case_law.why_it_matters: Included as the leading safe-port and subrogated-recourse authority, not as a war-risk coverage case. It is what happens after a hull insurer pays and then tries to recover from the charterer. Gard sued as H&M insurer and assignee, and lost.
case_law.note: Recorded here with an explicit caveat: this is a recourse case, not a coverage case. Do not cite it for whether a war-risk claim gets paid.

case_law.case: Whether a Houthi attack is an act of war, terrorism or a malicious act
case_law.issue: Which exclusion or insured peril a Houthi missile or drone strike falls under. This determines who pays on every Red Sea loss in this dataset.
case_law.held: No published court or arbitration decision, 2023 to 2026. Searched extensively and specifically.
case_law.why_it_matters: The single largest hole in the legal record. Practitioner commentary reports that disputes at the intersection of war risk, sanctions and charterparty obligations are already flowing into arbitration in Singapore and London — but London and Singapore maritime arbitration is confidential and unreported, so this may never surface publicly. The nearest usable analogue is the Russian Aircraft Lessor judgment.
case_law.note: Recorded as a case-law entry on purpose. The absence is the finding.

claims.what: Galaxy Leader hull war risk policy
claims.label: $65m
claims.payer: Ascot, Markel, Swiss Re, Arch, Skuld, Tokio Marine HCC, Ark
claims.note: Constructive total loss declared on deprivation of use beyond twelve months. Owner reported as set to collect. Payment never publicly confirmed, and a separate loss-of-hire dispute with Codan is unresolved.

claims.what: Rubymar hull claim, now in litigation
claims.label: $5m
claims.note: Berytus Insurance & Reinsurance SAL v Golden Adventure Shipping SA [2025] EWHC 664 (Comm). The insurer sued first, on 17 August 2024, for negative declaratory relief; the owner's defence was lodged 7 July 2025. Insurers deny liability. Only the jurisdiction ruling is public — the merits are undecided.

claims.label: about $80m
claims.note: Vessel and roughly a million barrels of crude were saved, so no hull total loss claim arose. The salvage was funded by the vessel's insurers over 135 days with more than 200 personnel and seven salvage vessels. The cost has never been disclosed.

claims.label: $93.6m
claims.note: Media estimate relayed by Clyde & Co, not a verified figure. The parties took a wait-and-see approach as the one-year Marine Insurance Act s.60 constructive total loss mark approached. No payout confirmed. Iranian prosecutors separately sought a $170m fine from Zodiac Maritime.

claims.what: Eternity C loss, borne by the owner
claims.label: about $20m
claims.note: Nothing was paid. Travelers, the vessel's usual war risk insurer, declined to extend cover before the passage and the vessel sailed without it. Four crew died.

claims.label: about $37m
claims.note: Clarksons valuation via Bloomberg. A vessel value, not a claim. Lloyd's List separately reported a $40m loss and a salvage claim likely above $2m, with lead underwriter Travelers not having posted security.

claims.what: Lloyd's of London net losses from the Middle East conflict
claims.label: £1.4bn / $1.9bn
claims.note: Half-year 2026 results, covering the period from 28 February 2026. CFO Jim Bichard confirmed £1.4bn is net and gross is larger. CEO Patrick Tiernan: 'we do not currently expect the situation to constitute a capital event.' Hardest-hit classes were marine, energy and political violence. Lloyd's activated its major event response group in early March 2026.

claims.what: Marine insurer claims from the Gulf conflict
claims.label: $1.5-2bn across about 70 casualties
claims.note: Lars Lange, Secretary General of IUMI, via Lloyd's List. David Osler puts it at roughly $2bn across 70+ claims and calls it the second-biggest payout for marine underwriters in more than a decade, exceeded only by the Baltimore bridge in 2024.

claims.what: Red Sea campaign 2023-2025 as a market loss event
claims.label: no major loss event recorded
claims.note: Lloyd's full-year 2025 results name no Red Sea major loss event at all. The major-claims narrative runs Ukraine 2022, then Hurricane Ian, then Milton, Helene and Beryl. Major claims ratio was 5.8% in 2025 against a ten-year average of 10.4%. IUMI's Secretary General said in March 2024 that losses remained within underwriting tolerance. The 2023-25 Red Sea campaign was not a market loss event. The 2026 Iran war is.

claims.label: about $1bn a year
claims.note: London alone put at about £500m by Marsh McLennan; the ~$1bn global figure comes from two unnamed insurance officials. Bloomberg notes there is no industry-standard measure of war-risk premium written, so no formal loss ratio exists. Treat every profitability claim in this area as qualitative.

claims.label: $5m
claims.note: Hijacked 12 March 2024 with 23 crew and 55,000 tonnes of coal; released 14 April. Sourced to two named pirates; cash airdropped in three sacks. Owner KSRM has never publicly confirmed it. The only confirmed ransom payment in this dataset.

claims.label: nothing paid
claims.note: Retaken by the Indian Navy after a 40-hour operation; 35 pirates surrendered. A military resolution, not a payment. Recorded explicitly because the Ruen and the Abdullah are routinely conflated — the $5m was the Abdullah.

claims.what: Galaxy Leader crew release — no ransom
claims.label: nothing paid
claims.note: Twenty-five seafarers held 430 days, released via Omani mediation. A political release, not a kidnap-and-ransom settlement.

claims.label: $39.92bn
claims.note: IUMI Stats Report 2025, data year 2024, up 1.5% on 2023. Cargo $22.64bn, ocean hull $9.67bn, offshore energy down 8%. Cargo loss ratios improved for a sixth consecutive year.

claims.what: Cargo vessels and value trapped in the Persian Gulf
claims.label: $125bn across ~1,150 vessels
claims.note: Roughly 1,150 cargo vessels, 29m gross tonnes, combined vessel and cargo value about $125bn, as at 15 June 2026. The IMO recorded 46 merchant vessels damaged in the conflict as at 11 June 2026. Underwriters warn of multibillion-dollar total-loss liabilities if trapped vessels reach the twelve-month deprivation-of-use threshold.

claims.what: Potential oil spill cleanup from a shadow-fleet tanker
claims.label: up to $1.6bn
claims.note: The reason uninsured tonnage is a systemic problem and not just a commercial one. With 36.5% of the tanker fleet carrying no verifiable cover, there may be no solvent payer.

claims.what: War-risk insurance embedded in the crude oil price
claims.label: $7-8 a barrel
claims.note: David Osler, Lloyd's List. Where the cost actually lands: not on the shipowner, but on the consumer.

figures.note: Up 1.5%. Cargo $22.64bn (56.7%), ocean hull $9.67bn (24.2%), offshore energy $4.34bn (10.9%), marine liability the balance. IUMI's own narrative text gives a different split from its chart; only the chart set reconciles with the dollar amounts.

figures.metric: Marine war as a share of the marine market
figures.note: The IUA's London company market figure of 2.5% and Howden Re's 2-3% agree independently. War risk is a rounding error in the marine market that determines whether trade moves at all.

figures.metric: Marine war premium, London company market
figures.note: The only discrete marine war premium line anyone publishes. Read it as a floor: it excludes Lloyd's entirely, excludes London-controlled business written elsewhere, and the IUA's methodology pushes un-split returns into 'Other'.

figures.metric: Share of world ocean-going tonnage covered by the International Group
figures.note: The IG's About page says 87% twice in body text. The widely-quoted 90% survives only in the site-wide HTML meta description — most 90% citations are quoting a meta tag.

figures.metric: Tonnage insured by the International Group

figures.note: A record, up $850m or 14.3%. Club-reported figures differ from broker comparable-basis figures for several clubs; neither is wrong.

figures.metric: Cover above the individual club retention
figures.note: $2.25bn of group excess of loss above a $100m pool ceiling, plus $1bn of collective overspill. AXA XL leads. The pooling agreement shares claims to about $8.9bn.

figures.metric: Global tanker fleet with no identifiable insurance
figures.note: 5,134 vessels of roughly 14,000. Only 29.4% of tankers carrying Russian crude in 2024 had International Group cover, against more than 90% for tankers carrying only non-Russian cargo.

figures.unit: percent of hull value per transit
figures.note: Up from 0.10-0.15% before the war began on 28 February 2026, and about 2.5% at the March peak. $10.5-14m on a VLCC. This settles a long-standing flag in this library: the figure is right and needed only a date.

figures.metric: Lloyd's marine war underwriters still writing hull war
figures.note: Over 90% still writing cargo. The LMA's own statement: reports that cover was cancelled or unaffordable, and that this is why vessels stopped transiting Hormuz, are 'not accurate'. The binding constraint was crew safety.

figures.metric: US ocean marine direct premiums written
figures.note: Industry total, down 0.6%. AIG leads on $817.7m. US statutory only — not comparable with IUMI's global figure. Note also that US 'inland marine' is a statutory line covering goods in transit and contractors' equipment, and is not maritime at all.

why_it_is_opaque: Insurers are named when a London market lead exists and Lloyd's List, Insurance Day or The Insurer choose to report the slip, or when litigation forces disclosure. There is no third route. Every named insurer in this dataset traces back to four publishers or one court.
Vessels outside the London market stay opaque. Rubymar, Abdullah, Ruen and shadow-fleet tonnage yielded nothing, and they are exactly the hulls where cover is most likely to be absent or fictitious.

Settlements are never published. Insured values, claims filed and constructive total loss declarations are on the record; what was actually paid is not. No confirmed settled payment amount exists for any vessel here.
Arbitration is confidential. London and Singapore maritime arbitration is unreported, so the disputes that would tell us how Red Sea losses are actually being resolved may never surface.
Reputable publishers contradict each other on the same slip, and neither is checkable without a subscription. Both readings are recorded rather than one being chosen.
The market does not disclose its own size by company. No premium-based global ranking of marine insurers exists, and no broker publishes marine revenue or market share.
gaps: No confirmed settled payment amount for any vessel in this dataset. Insurers do not publish settlements.
The UK P&I club that arranged the Abdullah's $5m ransom is never named in any source, in any language. Likely protected by non-disclosure.
No insurer identified for Ruen, Hellas Aphrodite, MSC Aries, Marlin Luanda or Chem Pluto, despite extensive searching. See what_we_tried on each record.

No published court or arbitration decision, 2023 to 2026, on whether a Houthi attack is an act of war, terrorism or a malicious act. This is the question that decides who pays on every Red Sea loss here.
The outcome of the Galaxy Leader constructive total loss claim and the Codan loss-of-hire dispute is unknown, as is whether the $65m was ever paid.
The Rubymar litigation is decided only on jurisdiction. The merits are undecided.
The Sounion salvage cost has never been disclosed, though the insurers funded it.
No documented instance of a P&I club actually voiding cover for a false Russian price-cap attestation, though Gard, West of England and the American Club all say they would.
Lloyd's claims to be a recognised global leader in war risk and publishes no capacity figure and no syndicate count for it. It does not break out marine at all.
Participating syndicates in the Chubb and Beazley 2026 war consortia are not disclosed.
Ingosstrakh's insured vessel list is deliberately undisclosed. Only the Andromeda Star is documented.
Whether the DFC facility required US-flag status is unknown — the eligibility criteria were never published, and a US senator's request for them went unanswered.
open_questions: Does any underwriter discount for an escort, and who has to certify it? Without a broker willing to write the discount, an escort's value has to come entirely out of the routing saving. This remains the single most commercially important unanswered question in the library.

Who actually buys — the owner, the charterer, or the underwriter? Under most charters the charterer bears the war-risk premium, so the party with the budget may not be the party with the ship. An escort sold to a shipowner may be sold to the wrong person.

Is there a product in underwriting the gap rather than closing it? Eternity C was destroyed after its insurer declined the voyage. Cosmoship bore roughly $20m alone. Who serves the owner an underwriter has just walked away from?

Could an escort change the JWC listed-area boundary rather than the premium? The circular is what turns a geography into a price, and it moved the Red Sea line 7.5 degrees north in a single revision. Influencing the boundary is worth more than influencing a rate.

The denial decision moved upstream to the reinsurers in 2026, twice. If reinsurers cancel on 72 hours' notice, the customer for risk reduction may be the reinsurance layer and not the shipowner at all.

What is a verified escort worth against a fraudulent insurance certificate? Over 90% of shadow-fleet ships produce a certificate on demand; 36.5% of the tanker fleet has no verifiable cover. Verification, not protection, may be the sellable product.

The US government built a $40bn facility for unavailability and the actual problem was price and crew safety, so it wrote nothing. What would a product aimed at crew safety rather than at cover have sold?
